title: The Heating Wire
summary: Heat elements and thermometers to find how resistance changes with temperature, then power and energy bills.
subject: physics
concepts: Steady temperature of a heating element
learningOutcome: The student can use the temperature coefficient of resistance for heaters and thermometers, and find power, resistance and energy cost from P = VI = V²/R.

levels.title: Hot and cold
levels.adds: Baseline: R₂ = R₁[1 + α(T₂ − T₁)] forwards, and inverted to find the temperature from a steady current (Ex 3.3, Example 3.3).
hints: The fractional rise in resistance is α times the rise in temperature.
If the temperature is the unknown, first get the hot resistance from V/I.

levels.title: The toaster
levels.adds: New idea: the switch-on current gives the cold resistance, the steady current gives the hot one, and P = VI (Ex 3.6).
hints: Cold resistance is V divided by the switch-on current; hot resistance is V divided by the steady current.
The steady temperature follows from the change in resistance and α.
Steady power uses the steady current.

levels.title: The platinum thermometer
levels.adds: New idea: temperature from fixed points, and α from the same two readings (Ex 3.5, Example 3.4).
hints: The resistance rises linearly: t is 100 times the fraction of the way from R₀ to R₁₀₀.
Give α in units of 10⁻³ per °C.

levels.title: A weak supply
levels.adds: More steps: R = V²/P from the rating, then the power at a lower voltage (Section 3.9).
hints: The rating tells you the power at its working voltage: use P = V²/R to find R.
The resistance stays the same at the lower voltage.
The power then depends on the square of the voltage.

levels.title: The electricity bill
levels.adds: Apply it: energy in kilowatt-hours is power in kW times the hours (Section 3.9).
hints: Convert each power to kilowatts before multiplying by the hours.
Add up the kWh for every appliance.
The cost is the total kWh times the price of one kWh.

misconceptions: Resistance of a metal falls as it heats up
The current in a heater stays the same after switch-on
Power is proportional to voltage, not voltage squared
A kilowatt-hour is a unit of power
